processing: A cultivar rather than a finished tea, so processing depends on the maker. Early-sprouting Sichuan cultivars usually go into pan-fired or roller-fixed green tea, and that is the use reported for Mingshan Zao.
harvest_season: An early-budding plant, so as with other early Sichuan green tea cultivars the prized picking is the first spring flush.
appearance_dry: Varies with the maker; early-spring Sichuan greens are typically small, fine and fresh green.
appearance_liquor: Typical of Sichuan spring greens, a pale yellow-green and clear.
appearance_wet: Typically tender buds and young leaves in fresh green.
taste_profile: No tasting notes specific to this cultivar are documented; Sichuan spring greens in general run fresh and lightly vegetal with a soft sweetness.

brewing.notes: General advice for a tender spring green: a glass or an open gaiwan, water well off the boil, and no lid left on between steeps.

vintage_note: Tea from this cultivar is not usually sold under its own name, and no specific sale pattern is documented. As is usual for Chinese greens, whatever is made from it is sold as the current spring harvest, with the earliest pickings costing more.
description:
Mingshan Zao 311 is a tea plant cultivar named after Mingshan, the tea district of Ya'an in Sichuan. 'Zao' means early, and the number looks like a selection code. It is a plant more than a product, so you are more likely to meet it in a grower's records than on a shop label.

Very little about this exact selection is documented in the open. A field trial published in 2004 tested a cultivar called simply Mingshan Zao in the Xinyang area of Henan, with Fuding Dabai as the control. It budded about as early as the control, matched it for yield and for cold and drought resistance, and was judged suitable for green tea. The paper gives no number, so it may or may not be this same selection.

No taste notes for the cultivar itself are on record. If you find a green tea made from it, expect what is typical of early Sichuan spring green: fresh, lightly vegetal and gently sweet. Brew it as you would any tender green, with cooler water and short contact.

A label naming this cultivar is worth a question to the seller about where and when the tea was picked, since the cultivar alone tells you little about the cup.
history: Where, when and by whom this selection was bred is not well documented, beyond the link to Mingshan its name implies. The clearest published trace of the name is the 2004 trial of Mingshan Zao as a new cultivar for tea areas north of the Yangtze, though that paper does not use the number 311.
